paras: Every evening, for a little over a century, someone in a city like this did exactly what she's doing:
walked out at dusk with a ladder and a long pole, and gave the street its night.
Ida isn't real.
Her city has no name.
But her job was real, and so are the numbers you're about to hear.
This is a story about that job:
how it began, how fast it grew, how it ended, and the handful of people who still do it.
And at the end, a question about the jobs we do today.

paras: Our story starts in London, in 1807, on a single street:
Pall Mall.
An inventor named Frederick Winsor ran pipes along it and lit a row of lamps burning coal gas.
It is remembered as the first street in the world lit that way.
People came out just to stare at it.
In 1812 the world's first gas company received its royal charter.
A year later, Westminster Bridge was glowing.
And then the thing spread the way good ideas and bad smells do:
quickly.
By the 1820s, London had more than forty thousand gas lamps along some two hundred and fifteen miles of street.
Forty thousand.
Hold on to that number; we'll come back to it.
Forty thousand lamps don't light themselves.
Every one of them needed a person.

paras: A lamplighter's evening was called a round.
You lit dozens of lamps at dusk, one after another along a fixed route, then walked the same route at dawn to put them out.
In between, the job was more than fire.
You cleaned the glass, reported the broken ones, and knew, without a map, which corner always went out first in the wind.
Rain, fog, frost:
it didn't matter.
If the lamps on your round weren't lit by the time people noticed the dark, people noticed you.
Forty thousand lamps meant a small army walking the streets every dusk and every dawn.

paras: The idea crossed the Atlantic fast.
In 1816 a painter, Rembrandt Peale, lit a room of his Baltimore museum with gas, as a kind of show.
Within a year, on the seventh of February 1817, Baltimore lit America's first public gas street lamp.
Paris took its time and then went all in.
By the middle of the century its boulevards ran on gas.

paras: Then came a different kind of light.
In 1878, for the World's Fair, Paris strung sixty-four electric arc lamps along and around the Avenue de l'Opéra.
They were harsh and blue-white, and they did not need anybody on a ladder.
Two years later, in 1880, New York put electric lights on Broadway.
At first, gas held on.
Electricity was new, expensive, sometimes unreliable.
But each white lamp that went up was one less stop on somebody's round, and the people doing the rounds could count.
It was a slow tide, not a single night:
a white lamp on the main avenue one year, a few more on the side streets the next, until the round got shorter.
Ida's watch runs seven minutes slow, and she knows it.
That's the feeling we wanted:
the city's clock moving on, and someone still walking on the old time.

paras: In April 1907, New York's lamplighters went on strike.
They worked for the private company that lit the streets that still had no electric lamps, and they wanted their union recognised and better pay.
The next morning's papers reported parts of the city in darkness.
Police officers were sent out to light the lamps themselves, some of them climbing the posts with matches.
Within about a week, the men were back at work.
But the strike made something plain.
A strike only works if the city can't do without you.
And every year, the city could do a little more without them.

paras: Over the next half century the gas lamps went out, city by city, lamp by lamp, contract by contract.
In New York, only two lampposts from the gas era still stand.
Paris, the city of light, took down its last gas street lamps in 1962.
And London, where it all began with forty thousand lamps?
London did something unusual.
It kept some.

paras: Here's the part most people don't know.
London still has gas street lamps:
in Covent Garden, along the Mall, outside palaces and theatres.
In 2015, there were about fifteen hundred of them.
By British Gas's own count in 2023, its team looks after about eleven hundred.
And that team is five people.
Five lamplighters.
They don't carry fire anymore.
Most of the lamps run on small clockwork timers, and every two weeks someone climbs up to wind the clock and check the lamp.
When Westminster proposed swapping its gas lamps for LEDs in 2022, residents objected.
In 2024, four lamps in Covent Garden, put up in 1910, were formally listed as protected heritage.
Forty thousand lamps, once.
About eleven hundred now.
Five people.

paras: We gave Ida an ending the real lamplighters mostly didn't get.
She gets to choose her last lamp.
For the real ones, it was a new contract, or a white post on the route one morning, and the round was gone.
History doesn't record most of their names.
What Ida keeps isn't the job.
It's the small warm thing the job was for, and she hands it on.
Cas will never light a street.
He'll grow up in the white city.
But he knows how to warm his hands at a lamp and count to three, because somebody showed him.

paras: Lamplighting was an extreme case:
a job that was almost entirely one task, and a switch could do it.
The economist James Bessen took about two hundred and seventy occupations from the 1950 U.S. Census and followed them to 2010.
Plenty disappeared, often because people stopped needing them, like telegraph operators.
But only one vanished mainly because a machine took over the work:
the elevator operator.
One in two hundred and seventy.
Machines mostly took tasks, not whole jobs.

paras: So who is on that list today?
Every year, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects how American jobs will change over the next ten years.
The newest, published in August 2026, cover 2025 to 2035.
Top of the fastest-shrinking list:
word processors and typists, projected to fall by about thirty-four percent.
Then telephone operators, down nearly twenty-eight percent; only about three and a half thousand are left.
Switchboard operators and data entry keyers, each down about a quarter.
Telemarketers, down about a fifth.
What they share:
much of the work is one repeated task, and automation tools, including AI, are taking on more of it.
These are forecasts, not verdicts.
But the pattern sounds familiar.

paras: In an earlier round, for 2023 to 2033, BLS spelled out where it expects AI to reduce demand:
customer service representatives down five percent, auto damage appraisers down about nine.
But software developers up almost eighteen.
AI changes work; it doesn't only remove it.
And the newest list has fast-growing jobs too:
nurse practitioners, solar installers, data scientists, wind turbine technicians, each up about thirty percent or more.
One early warning.

Stanford's Digital Economy Lab found that, by June 2026, employment of workers aged twenty-two to twenty-five in the jobs most exposed to AI was about nineteen percent below where it would otherwise be, mostly because fewer were hired.
Experienced workers showed no such gap.
The researchers call it an early signal, not proof that AI caused it.
